messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sameer, a 49-year-old military medic, presented as a man holding himself rigidly, as if bracing for a blow that never came. For over a year, he had been living in the aftershock of a severe assault by his former partner. The attack had happened in their shared home, a place of supposed safety, escalating from a verbal argument into a physical onslaught that left him with fractured ribs and a profound sense of bewilderment. He remembers the cloying smell of his partner’s sweat, the feeling of being overpowered, and the chilling silence of his partner’s relatives who were present in the next room and did nothing to intervene. When he finally managed to call the police, their response was dismissive, their questions laced with an implicit disbelief that he, a man in uniform, could be a victim. This initial failure of accountability laid the groundwork for a deep and pervasive cynicism.

In the months that followed, Sameer’s world began to shrink. The memory of the assault was not a coherent narrative he could recount; instead, it was a series of sensory fragments that ambushed him without warning. He found he simply could not put the event into words, a frustrating silence that felt like a personal failing. At his army base, a sudden loud noise would cause him to flinch violently, his heart hammering as a flash of the memory—the feeling of being pinned down—would surge through him. This constant sense of being on high alert made it impossible to rest; he would lie awake for hours at night, certain that he needed to stay vigilant to prevent another attack. On nights when this sense of threat was highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay, as if the adrenaline itself pulled the sensory fragments of the assault to the surface, unbidden and vivid. The feeling of being unsafe became so pervasive that his life contracted to two locations: his new apartment and the base. These were the only places he believed he could let his guard down, even slightly. Feeling this afraid all the time quietly confirmed the harsh judgment he had passed on himself: that this constant fear was simply proof of his own weakness, and that a capable man would not feel so perpetually terrified.

The triggers were everywhere. The sight of a police car would send a wave of hot anger and helplessness through him, reinforcing his belief that the people responsible had faced no consequences and that the system was broken. Seeing any of his ex-partner’s relatives in town would cause his breath to catch, and the memory would return not as a thought but as a physical sensation—a sharp, phantom pain blooming in his ribs, exactly where the blows had landed. The memory felt so immediate, so viscerally real, that it was as if the assault were happening all over again. These intrusive experiences invariably led to a cascade of self-recrimination; he came to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him, that a stronger man would have fought back more effectively, or would have moved on by now. This conviction that he was fundamentally flawed transformed the world into a place of constant potential danger, as he was certain he lacked the capacity to protect himself from another attack. This appraisal of being a defective person made the memory itself feel even more toxic and shameful, something to be walled off rather than processed.

This deep-seated sense of personal failure and the constant feeling of threat drove Sameer to systematically dismantle his own life. To avoid the agonizing, relived pain of the memory, he began to avoid anything that might evoke it. He stopped exercising, unable to bear the smell of sweat in the gym, which instantly transported him back to the attack. He threw out the clothes he had been wearing that night and scrupulously avoided anything of a similar style. The belief that he was flawed and that people could see it made him withdraw from friends and colleagues, until he was almost completely isolated. This avoidance, however, only tightened the trap. By staying home, his world shrank further, which reinforced his belief that only a few places were truly safe. The isolation gave him more time to ruminate on his perceived inadequacies, making the traumatic memory the central, defining fact of his existence. His hypervigilance, born of a constant sense of threat, made him scan his environment for danger, which paradoxically made him even more likely to spot triggers, like a passing police car, thereby initiating the cycle anew.

His wife, Maria, watched him become a ghost in their home, a man perpetually startled and withdrawn. His work, once a source of pride, began to suffer. He was jumpy around patients, his focus fractured. It was after he recoiled from a patient who needed urgent help, simply because the man’s body odour triggered a flashback, that Maria insisted he seek therapy. Sameer agreed, not with hope, but with a sense of exhausted defeat. He feels that nothing in his life is meaningful anymore; the competent, caring medic he once was has been replaced by this fragile, frightened stranger. He is terrified that this is who he is now, and that the man he used to be is gone for good.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not state that the trauma memory causes or leads to a sense of threat.
